why: The author kept the neural-pathways sentences as his own first-person voice; A's version is the thinner cut.
A keeps the clause about what a mismatch means, which gives the student a concrete way to act on the spot-check; B is shorter but leaves the check without a result.
Cuts the parenthetical recap of M6 and the closing slogan ('That is the flywheel'); fewer words, no clever kicker.
Shorter; B adds words ('for the pushback', 'this session's') that add little.
Author cuts course-structure sentences like the forward pointer to Phases 3 and 4 as low-value.
B adds a sentence about the course itself ('you are not learning them here'), which the author cuts as orientation.
B names what the slide covers in plain words; A's title is a count, which the author cuts when the number does no memory work.
A names the concrete steps of the Module 1 loop so the agent checks the right things, and B's 'git status is clean' could claim something not always true.
A's opening fragment 'A strong candidate for a team PR, after you talk to the team' is a low-value restatement of the heading; B opens on the concrete skill and has fewer words.
'Loop it, instead of you starting it' puts the stronger concept (looping) in the heading and opens on what the student does, per the author's own call.
The author kept the advanced statusline option on a basic step: teach the best current practice, not just the built-in.
The header names the concrete point in plain words, where A's abstract 'agentic knowledge compounds' repeats the first body sentence.

The title "Five things a good plan has" is an orienting count and the author keeps counts here as a frame; A's retitle drops the count with no clear gain, while B's title is also clearer and more concrete.

The permission line "You don't need to get it right first time" is the author's own permission framing (duty becomes permission) and reinforces the experiment stance, matching his kept line in tn-permission-testing about duplication and the why of experimenting.
Cuts the orientation lines about the map and what each lecture names; course-about-itself and forward-hint sentences go.
Shorter; the added sentence only restates that the output over-produces and adds no new information.
B cuts the 'judgement in your hands' closer and the 'theatre' put-down sentence; fewer words, and the author cuts closers and clever lines.
The only difference is the added bold lead-ins; plain A is shorter and avoids bold-heavy slogan-style emphasis, matching the author's neutral register.
Text is identical; bolding the lead-ins adds visual noise with no stated reason, so the plain version reads cleaner.
